common_name: Lennon's Song Cast Iron Plant (Fine Cream-Speckled Deep-Shade Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to full shade; keep evenly watered the first season while the rhizome establishes.

directions: Plant in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic to neutral soil in partial to deep shade, where the leathery, strap-shaped leaves hold their finest markings. Lennon's Song is a cast iron plant selection prized for its dense, fine cream-to-white speckling scattered across the dark green leaf surface, a more delicate, freckled pattern than the bold stripes of 'Variegata' or the coarse spotting of 'Stars and Stripes'. Like other Aspidistra elatior selections it is exceptionally tough once established, shrugging off root competition from mature trees, long dry spells, and heavy shade that would kill most other perennials. Growth and clump expansion are slow, so plant divisions at final spacing rather than expecting quick fill-in, and reserve occasional light feeding and supplemental water for the establishment year only.

common_name: Star Frost Cast Iron Plant (Fine White-Speckled Sichuan Aspidistra)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in spring or fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in full shade to deep shade; slow to establish, so keep evenly moist through the first year and avoid disturbing the clump once settled.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in humus-rich, well-drained soil in full to deep shade, watering regularly while the clump establishes and only occasionally once mature. Star Frost carries the narrow, slender leaves typical of Aspidistra sichuanensis, each finely and evenly dusted overall with small frosty-white speckles, giving a softer, more uniform silvered effect across the whole leaf than the larger, sparser blotches of the related 'Ginga'. It spreads gradually by rhizome into a dense, low, weed-suppressing clump and keeps its markings and glossy dark green base color year-round in deep shade positions where few flowering perennials can compete. As with other Aspidistra species it is extremely tough and essentially maintenance-free once established, making it a good choice for a shaded path edge or container where its fine speckling can be seen up close.

common_name: White-Edged Dwarf Lily Turf (Variegated Ophiopogon intermedius)

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; establishes faster than most mondo grasses and spreads by short rhizomes into a tidy tufted clump.

directions: Plant divisions in moist, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial to full shade, watering regularly until new growth shows the clump has taken hold. This cultivar of Ophiopogon intermedius forms grassy tufts noticeably larger than dwarf mondo grass (Ophiopogon japonicus) but smaller than white lily-turf (Ophiopogon jaburan), with each slender, arching leaf edged in a crisp white margin against a dark green center, giving a bright, fine-textured accent along shaded paths and bed edges. It spreads slowly by short rhizomes to form a dense, weed-suppressing tuft rather than running aggressively, so it stays well-behaved as a border planting or small-scale groundcover. Small pale lilac flower spikes appear in summer on established clumps but are secondary to the variegated foliage, which holds its color year-round in evergreen zones.

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; variegation and flower spike size are both best in a few hours of direct or bright filtered light.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing clumps to allow the arching foliage to display fully. John Burch is a Liriope muscari cultivar selected for two traits at once: leaves striped lengthwise in gold and green rather than solid dark green, and unusually tall, dense flower spikes in violet-purple that rise well above the foliage in late summer, larger than those of most other variegated liriope cultivars. The combination of bright variegated foliage and a bold bloom display makes it a stronger focal accent than plain green liriope, useful for breaking up large monotone groundcover plantings under high shade trees. Like other liriope it tolerates heat, humidity, and periodic drought once established, and clumps can be divided every three to five years as they become crowded.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container plants in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; give extra spacing compared to standard liriope since the broad foliage clump reaches full size quickly.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, allowing extra room for the wide, arching leaves to spread. Webster Wideleaf is a vigorous Liriope muscari selection with markedly broader, deeper glossy-green leaf blades than standard liriope cultivars, giving a coarser, bolder texture in mass plantings and borders. Dense spikes of deep violet-purple flowers rise above the foliage in late summer, followed by black berries that persist into winter. The broad leaves and robust habit make it a strong groundcover choice for filling large shaded areas quickly, and established clumps tolerate the same range of heat, humidity, and drought stress as other liriope once settled in.

common_name: Franklin Mint Creeping Liriope (Purple-Flowered Spreading Lilyturf)

planting.note: Plant divisions or plugs in spring in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade; spreads by stolons like the parent species, so contain with edging where a running groundcover is not wanted.

directions: Plant divisions or plugs in moist to moderately dry, well-drained soil in full sun to full shade, spacing to account for its spreading habit. Franklin Mint is a creeping lilyturf selection valued for producing noticeably more visible violet-purple flower spikes than the straight species, which typically blooms sparsely or has its flowers hidden beneath the foliage; here the spikes stand out clearly against the narrow, dark green leaves in late summer. It spreads by stolons to form a dense, running groundcover mat that suppresses weeds and tolerates the same wide range of soil, moisture, and light conditions as ordinary Liriope spicata, from deep shade under trees to full sun in average garden soil. Because it spreads more assertively than clumping Liriope muscari cultivars, install edging or a mowed strip where a contained bed rather than a colonizing mat is the goal.

common_name: Emerald Goddess Liriope (Large Vigorous Clumping Lilyturf)

planting.note: Plant container plants or divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun; the large, vigorous clump needs more room than standard liriope and is slower to require division.

directions: Plant in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in partial shade to full sun, spacing generously since the clump grows noticeably larger than standard Liriope muscari over time. Emerald Goddess is a patented, vigorous liriope hybrid selected for wide, glossy dark green leaves, a large and uniform clump habit, and improved resistance to the leaf-spot and crown-rot problems that trouble some older liriope cultivars in hot, humid climates. Tall spikes of pale lavender to violet flowers rise above the foliage in summer, followed by black berries, and the bold, upright form reads more like a small ornamental grass than typical low liriope groundcover. It is markedly slower to need dividing than smaller cultivars, tolerates heat, humidity, and drought once established, and performs well in both shaded borders and container plantings.
